cls: Antiprotozoal / antiparasitic - dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (folic acid antagonist)
quick: Toxoplasmosis: loading ~100-200 mg, then 50-75 mg/day with sulfadiazine + leucovorin
Take with meals to reduce GI upset
Avoid in 1st trimester (teratogen); always co-give leucovorin
Excreted in milk; co-administer leucovorin; weigh risk
Use with caution; reduce dose in impairment
CBC with platelets (twice weekly at high dose), folate, LFTs
summary: Pyrimethamine is a folic acid antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking synthesis of tetrahydrofolate in susceptible protozoa. It is used (with a sulfonamide such as sulfadiazine) to treat toxoplasmosis and, historically, for malaria treatment and prophylaxis. Its main toxicity is dose-dependent bone marrow suppression from folate depletion, which is mitigated by co-administering leucovorin (folinic acid) to protect host cells.
indications: Treatment of toxoplasmosis, in combination with a sulfonamide (e.g., sulfadiazine)
Treatment of acute malaria (with a fast-acting schizonticide), used adjunctively
Prophylaxis/suppression of malaria in areas where susceptible Plasmodium strains exist (historical use)

dosage.d: Loading 50-100 mg (up to 200 mg) then 25-75 mg once daily
dosage.n: With sulfadiazine and leucovorin (folinic acid) 10-25 mg/day; usually 1-3 weeks then reduce

dosage.d: Loading ~2 mg/kg/day x2-3 days, then 1 mg/kg/day
dosage.n: With sulfadiazine and leucovorin; max per labeling

dosage.d: 25 mg once daily for 2 days (with a fast schizonticide)

dosage.n: Children >10 yr 25 mg weekly; limited by resistance

admin: Take with food or meals to minimize gastrointestinal upset
ALWAYS co-administer leucovorin (folinic acid) at higher antitoxoplasma doses to prevent hematologic toxicity
Obtain baseline CBC and monitor blood counts (twice weekly during high-dose therapy)
Do not substitute folic acid for leucovorin - folic acid does not adequately protect against marrow toxicity and may reduce efficacy
Keep well out of reach of children - small overdoses can be fatal in children
moa: Pyrimethamine selectively inhibits protozoal dihydrofolate reductase, preventing reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and thereby blocking synthesis of nucleic acid precursors (purines and thymidylate) needed for parasite replication. Combination with a sulfonamide produces sequential blockade of the folate pathway for a synergistic antiparasitic effect.

absolute: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
relative: Pregnancy, especially first trimester (teratogenic in animals; co-give leucovorin)
Seizure disorder (use lower starting doses; convulsions reported)

preg: Crosses the placenta and is teratogenic in animals; avoid in the first trimester. When used in pregnancy for toxoplasmosis later in gestation, always co-administer leucovorin and weigh maternal benefit against fetal risk.
lact: Pyrimethamine is excreted into breast milk. If used during breastfeeding, co-administer leucovorin and monitor the infant; weigh benefits against potential harm, and avoid giving the infant additional folate antagonists.
renal: Use with caution and consider dose reduction in renal impairment, as elimination may be reduced and toxicity increased.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; monitor liver function during therapy.

major: Other folate antagonists (methotrexate, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, sulfonamides) - additive marrow suppression / megaloblastic anemia
Bone marrow suppressants (cytotoxics, zidovudine) - additive myelosuppression
moderate: Lorazepam - reports of hepatotoxicity in combination
minor: Drugs causing folate deficiency (phenytoin) - additive effect
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; ensure adequate folinic acid (leucovorin), not folic acid.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol to avoid additional marrow and hepatic stress.
interactions.diagnostics: Can lower blood counts (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and cause megaloblastic changes.

common: Anorexia and vomiting (dose-related, lessened by giving with meals)
serious: Bone marrow suppression - megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia
Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme) - especially with sulfonamide

monitoring: CBC with platelet count - twice weekly during high-dose antitoxoplasma therapy
Signs of folate deficiency (sore tongue, megaloblastic changes)
Skin for rash - stop at first sign of serious cutaneous reaction
counsel: Take with food to reduce nausea
Take the leucovorin (folinic acid) exactly as prescribed - it protects your blood cells; do not skip it
Report sore throat, fever, unusual bruising/bleeding, pallor or extreme tiredness (possible blood count drop)
Stop and seek care immediately for any rash, blistering or mouth sores
Keep this medicine well away from children - even small amounts can be very dangerous to them
pk: Antiparasitic effect develops over days of therapy
Plasma peak about 2-6 hours after an oral dose
Long half-life allows daily (toxoplasmosis) or weekly (malaria prophylaxis) dosing
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light
pearls: Folate antagonist - ALWAYS pair higher antitoxoplasma doses with leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue to protect host marrow; folic acid is NOT a substitute
Standard toxoplasmosis regimen is pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin
Very long half-life (~4 days) means toxicity can persist after stopping
Highly toxic to children in overdose - secure storage is essential
Widespread Plasmodium resistance has largely retired its antimalarial role except in fixed combinations
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it and resume the schedule. Do not double up. Continue leucovorin as prescribed.
overdose: Overdose causes vomiting, CNS stimulation with convulsions, and later megaloblastic bone marrow depression; it can be fatal, particularly in children. Management is supportive with gastric decontamination, seizure control (barbiturates/benzodiazepines), and leucovorin (folinic acid) in high doses for several days to counter marrow toxicity.
